newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike will test trend toward part-time workers.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike will test trend toward part-time workers.

text.p: The Teamsters strike against United Parcel Service is shaping up as a dramatic test of whether companies can expand their use of lower-wage part-time workers rather than full-time employees, experts said on Tuesday.

Labour experts said UPS typifies the new type of American company -- a service business that adds many part-time workers instead of secure full-time jobs that include expensive benefits such as health insurance and pensions.

The 185,000 Teamster workers at UPS are angry that three out of five of them have only part-time work, earning about half the hourly wages and only a fraction of the benefits earned by full-time workers.

The strike, in its second day Tuesday with no new talks scheduled, will be a crucial test for labour, which after withering for years is claiming renewed strength, and for UPS, the nation's largest package delivery company that is facing its first nationwide walkout in 90 years of doing business.

For the labour movement, which now covers only 10 percent of non-government workers, down from a peak of 38 percent in 1953, the strike represents a chance to show average Americans it can win a fight over the right to a decent working wage.
For UPS and the rest of corporate America, the fight is over the fundamental issue of how management runs its business in a competitive, fast-changing economy.

"It's the relationship with the employer that has changed," says Richard Hurd, professor of labour studies at Cornell University. "UPS has only a part-time commitment to the workers. That gives UPS a lot more flexiblity in scheduling, very similar to using a temporary help agency."

The strike has come at a particularly difficult time for the Teamsters union, which is under federal scrutiny for alleged fund-raising abuses by President Ron Carey, who was re-elected in a tight race last year. And the union's strike fund is depleted, making this far from the ideal time for a strike.

Government figures show that the percentage of part-time workers in the United States has stayed between 15 percent and 18 percent for decades, but experts said the figures do not account for big changes occurring in the workplace.
In many cases, so-called part-time workers are employed by UPS for full-time hours, the experts said.
Eileen Appelbaum, a labour economist and associate research director at the Economic Policy Institute in Washington, said wages have remained stagnant because of new fears about job security.

"Why at this stage of the business cycle are wages not rising?" she said. "The answer is that there is a tremendous anxiety. Even if you have a full-time job you are concerned that an employer might replace you with two part-time workers, an independent contractor, a temporary worker or outsourcing."
Hurd said those concerns drove a series of small strikes at General Motors plants where workers protested the use of small outside companies to do work, usually at lower cost.
Yet another way the same trend shows up is to fire people and hire them back as temps. Hurd said that AT&T slashed its staff, then hired many back on temporary contracts.
The same kinds of concerns over a long-term, stable employer committment were reflected in a bitter, 10-month strike by 4,500 steelworkers.

The United Steelworkers Union strike ended over the weekend when the union accepted a 19 percent reduction in the work force. In return, workers won a commitment from management to pay pensions at a fixed level instead of relying on pensions that vary with ups and downs in the stock market.
